rationale: B wins because it is more disciplined about proof and list control; three usable angles beat A's fourth angle wandering into made-up exclusivity. A's best line, "Liquid Death says it's profitable. It just won't say by how much," is a real business hook, but "sells water you can't buy anywhere else" is unsupported by the update. B's "A canned-water brand says it has given $4.2M to clean-water charities. Here's what that buys" has a cleaner reporter shape and a real evidence burden instead of a souvenir-shop SKU dressed up as news.
gaps_in_A: "Liquid Death's new store sells water you can't buy anywhere else — for now" invents exclusivity; the update says limited-edition canned water, not store-only or unavailable elsewhere.
"the limited-edition can launches alongside the store opening" adds a launch timing the facts do not give.
The fourth angle is thin beverage-trade padding; without proof that the can differs from normal SKUs or signals wider distribution, it is a merch drop with a can.
A's kept angles are strong, but the refused-angle discipline did not apply to its own product angle.
gaps_in_B: "Liquid Death opens a store that sells almost no water" is punchy, but overclaims the facts; no product-mix ratio proves "almost no water."
"an aluminum single-serve packaged-water brand" is a defensible inference from canned water, but still not explicitly supplied; the B Corp angle should flag that proof need sooner.
B leaves the contribution-margin/net-profit scrutiny as an uncomfortable question instead of keeping it as a fourth business/finance angle.
"There is no second one" is too absolute; the facts say first permanent location, not that no additional stores are planned.
